newsitem.title: USA: Gender gap becomes gulf in U.S. presidential race.
newsitem.headline: Gender gap becomes gulf in U.S. presidential race.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent
The so-called gender gap in U.S. politics has become a chasm in 1996, with polls suggesting women will make the difference for President Bill Clinton.
Polls over the past few months have shown a wide gap between the voting intentions of men and women, and that gap shows no sign of narrowing.

A Reuters poll last week gave the 50-year-old Democratic president a 10-point lead over Republican Bob Dole, 73, among men, and the two were running nearly even among white men. But among women, Clinton led by 20 points.
A Gallup poll last week showed Dole trailing by a single point among men, but by an astounding 32 points among women.
Conservative columnist Arianna Huffington said the gender gap, far from being a transient phenomenon, had become a fundamental feature of U.S. politics.
"The gender gap is fundamental thing because it points to a basic flaw in the Republican message," Huffington said.

"When women are asked about the economy, their answers have to do not only with their own pocketbooks but with the situation of people in need," she said. "When Republicans attacked government programmes, they were seen by women as shredding the social safety net."

That became clear in some two dozen interviews with voters conducted by Reuters last week, in which one woman after another expressed fear that Dole would allow valued social programmes to be dismantled if he were elected.
"I care about health care and education and Clinton cares about these things," said Katherine Nulty, who looks after her grandchildren in Port Richey, Florida.
"Dole is weak on social issues while Democrats are friendlier towards women. And abortion should be cut right out. I don't see where it's relevant," Nulty said.

In an opinion piece in Monday's Wall Street Journal, conservative ideologue Irving Kristol argued that there were important differences between the way men and women thought about key political and social problems.

"Women tend to be more sentimental, more risk-averse and less competitive than men -- yes, it's Mars vs Venus -- and therefore are less inclined to be appreciative of free-market economics (stressed by Republicans), in which there are losers and well as winners," Kristol wrote.

Ann Stone, who chairs the moderate Republicans for Choice pressure group that aims to persuade the party to drop its anti-abortion stance, said Republicans had lost the ability to communicate with women in terms they could understand.
"Men like charts and graphs, facts and figures. Women want to know how a particular problem affects their family, their children," Stone said.

Clinton is a master at stressing the effect of policies on people. He enjoys personal contact with voters, reveals his emotions and is constantly pictured hugging people. Dole, by contrast, appears uncomfortable even shaking hands.
It is not just how the candidates campaign, however, but the policies they stress that has accentuated the differences.
A classic example came on the hustings last weekend when Dole criticised a widely popular federal law letting workers take time off to care for a new baby or sick family member,
Clinton, who signed the measure early in his term, has called it one of his proudest achievements.

"My view is, why should the federal government be getting into family leave? It ought to be left to the employees or the state or the county and the federal government ought to be out of it," Dole said.
That invited a quick comeback from White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta, who said the act had helped almost 12 million families.
"Bob Dole is saying, 'Oh my God, we should not have the federal government participate in Family Leave or in education or in environment or in job training'," Panetta said.
"Ninety percent of the businesses say that it's right to be able to provide leave when you've got someone who's sick in the family, or someone who needs attention."
For some women, the abortion issue has become emblematic, of a party that advocates freedom from government control except where the reproductive rights of women are concerned.
"Women increasingly feel that Republicans don't understand their problems, don't value their part in society and want to put them back in the kitchen," said Stone.
